newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine shares extend slide on peso's woes.
newsitem.headline: Philippine shares extend slide on peso's woes.

text.p: Philippine shares slumped for the second straight day on Wednesday in the wake of the recent de facto peso devaluation and punishingly high interest rates.
The main share index sank below the 2,600 support level to close at 2,587.36, a drop of 68.50 points or 2.58 percent.

"This high interest rate is sapping liquidity out of the stock market to fixed-income securities. Hence, the selldown," said Jose Ricardo Garcia, executive vice-president at Diversified Securities Inc.

Commercial banks have roughly doubled interest rates in the past month and businessmen accused them of opportunism in the wake of the government's decision last Friday to allow the peso to trade in a wider range.
The move amounted to an effective devaluation, allowing the peso to fall about 12 percent against the dollar.
Some banks are charging rates as high as 35 percent but Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo told Reuters the high interest rates were merely a temporary problem.
"This is just a short-term phenomenon. We don't expect it to last a long time," he said.
The central bank, trying to defend the peso, has pushed its rates to their highest level since the Mexican financial crisis threatened to affect the Philippine economy in early 1995.
This time around, the "domino effect" is working in reverse and now beginning to hit markets in Latin America, including Mexico.
Central bank governor Gabriel Singson earlier warned that he would maintain a tight monetary policy until he felt the foreign exchange market had calmed down.
The Philippines last Friday became the latest country in the region to fall victim to currency speculators who have been hammering one Southeast Asian currency after another.
Thailand was forced into an effective devaluation earlier in the month and central banks in Malaysia and Indonesia have been battling to shield their currencies from the same fate.
Manila's central bank kept its promise in early trading to keep things under control and offloaded more dollars at 29 pesos.
At 0450 GMT, the peso was at 28.900 to the dollar.
But few local traders appeared to have the stamina to launch any fresh attacks on the peso.
Local banks, aware that the peso's woes were harming their own image, earlier made a "gentlemen's agreement" to limit falls in the peso to four percent.
The influential Federation of Philippine Industries said many commercial banks were "opportunistic and insensitive to their clients by taking advantage of the rapid depreciation of the peso".
In a statement, it demanded to know why banks were charging so much more to sell dollars than to buy them and why interest rates were so high.
The central bank has already started a witch-hunt to find out if any local banks were behind the relentless attacks on the peso.
The government has complained of "outside forces" being behind the peso plunge.
